stories.title: Williams offers Carlos Sainz $30 million a year to fend off Audi's interest for 2027
stories.what_happened: Williams has put forward a contract offer worth around **$30 million annually** to keep Carlos Sainz for the next two seasons, according to reports, as speculation mounted that he could leave for Audi in 2027. The offer is unusually large for a team not currently fighting at the front, reflecting how much Williams values Sainz's experience as it tries to climb the grid. Audi driver Gabriel Bortoleto has separately said his own future at Audi is already settled, undercutting the idea that a seat there is open for Sainz. Sainz has himself suggested since the Belgian Grand Prix that he's leaning toward staying at Williams, framing his priority as helping the team's 2027 push rather than chasing a move.
key_points: Williams has reportedly offered Sainz roughly **$30 million a year** to stay for two more seasons.
The move is aimed at heading off **Audi**, which had been seen as his likely destination for 2027.
Audi's existing driver **Gabriel Bortoleto** has already said his own seat there is 'sorted.'
Sainz himself has recently **hinted he plans to stay** at Williams, prioritizing helping the team improve for 2027.
The offer is described as a **'world champion's' pay package**, unusually large for Williams' current competitive position.

depth.background: Carlos Sainz joined Williams for 2025 after being replaced at Ferrari by Lewis Hamilton, and has been central to the team's attempt to rebuild toward the front of the grid. Audi is entering Formula 1 as a full works team from 2026 (having taken over the former Sauber team) and has been linked with poaching established drivers like Sainz to accelerate its competitiveness — but Audi's Bortoleto has pushed back on any suggestion he'd be dropped to make room.

stories.title: A wildfire shuts down California's Highway 1 and forces evacuations along the Sonoma Coast
stories.what_happened: The Woodside Fire was first reported around **1:40pm on Thursday**, burning along Highway 1 near Timber Cove on the Sonoma Coast. By about 6:40am Friday, crews had it **30% contained** after burning **143 acres**, helped by cooler nighttime temperatures and helicopter water drops. Highway 1 remains closed between Stewarts Point Skaggs Springs Road and Timber Cove Road. Evacuation orders are in place for Salt Point State Park and the Timber Cove area, including several coastal campgrounds, while an evacuation warning covers a wider inland zone. Smoke from the fire prompted the Bay Area Air District to issue a Spare the Air Alert for the wider region.
key_points: The **Woodside Fire** has burned **143 acres** along Highway 1 near Timber Cove and is **30% contained** as of Friday morning.
**Highway 1** — the region's main coastal road — remains closed between Stewarts Point Skaggs Springs Road and Timber Cove Road.
Evacuation orders cover **Salt Point State Park** and Timber Cove, with a wider evacuation warning stretching inland.
The Bay Area Air District issued a **Spare the Air Alert** as smoke from the fire blankets the region.
Cooler overnight conditions and helicopter water drops helped crews reach **30% containment** by Friday.

depth.background: Sonoma County's coastline sees wildfire risk every summer once vegetation dries out, and **Highway 1** is the only direct road through this stretch of coast, so any fire near it quickly disrupts travel for residents, campers and tourists. The fire is named the **Woodside Fire** and broke out along the coast near Timber Cove, a rural area dotted with state parkland and campgrounds. California's fire agencies, led by **CAL FIRE**, respond aggressively to coastal fires like this because wind can push them toward populated areas fast.

stories.title: South Korea's Kospi posts its biggest one-day gain ever as SK Hynix rockets 30% off the back of a brutal crash
stories.what_happened: On Friday, that panic reversed just as sharply as it began. The **Kospi**, South Korea's main stock index, jumped **17.9%** to **6,695.45** — its best single day on record — as **SK Hynix** shares rallied by the exchange's maximum allowed **30% daily limit** for the first time ever, and **Samsung Electronics** climbed roughly **27-28%**. The catalyst was a broader rebound in AI-related stocks on Wall Street overnight, which gave Korean investors confidence to buy back into memory-chip makers after the prior three-day, ~17% sell-off had erased tens of billions of dollars in value and triggered unprecedented back-to-back circuit-breaker halts. SK Hynix had fallen as much as **58% from its June 25 intraday peak** before Friday's rebound, meaning even after the historic bounce, the stock remains well below its highs.
key_points: The **Kospi index** jumped nearly **18%** on Friday to close at **6,695.45** — the single **biggest daily gain in its history**.
**SK Hynix** shares hit the exchange's **30% daily limit** (an automatic ceiling on how far a stock can move in one day) — the first time the stock has ever hit that ceiling.
**Samsung Electronics** surged roughly **27-28%** the same day.

The rally follows a **three-day, ~17% rout** in which SK Hynix fell as much as **58% from its June 25 peak**, triggering **back-to-back trading halts** (circuit breakers) on **July 28 and 29** — the first time that's ever happened on the Korean exchange.
The reversal tracked a bounce in **AI-linked stocks on Wall Street** after days of steep losses.

depth.background: Yesterday's brief covered how **SK Hynix and Samsung** had just posted **record AI-chip profits** — SK Hynix's operating profit jumped **557%** — only to see their stocks fall anyway, because investors worried the results still weren't good enough to justify sky-high AI valuations. That worry escalated fast: over the next three trading days, SK Hynix and Samsung shares were hammered, wiping out a huge chunk of their 2026 gains and forcing Korea's exchange to halt trading twice in a row for the first time ever, on July 28 and 29, as **circuit breakers** (automatic pauses designed to stop panic-selling) kicked in.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported that SK Hynix and Samsung posted record AI-chip profits (SK Hynix's operating profit up 557%) but their stocks fell anyway — a sign investors feared the AI-chip boom was overheating.
thread.changed: That fear spiraled into a three-day, ~17% crash with unprecedented back-to-back trading halts on July 28-29 — and then fully reversed today into the Kospi's best-ever single day, with SK Hynix hitting a 30% limit-up and Samsung surging ~27-28%.

stories.title: F1 shuts down for its mandatory summer break — no one is allowed to touch the cars for two weeks
stories.what_happened: From **July 31**, every Formula 1 team's factory closes its doors for a **mandatory two-week shutdown**, during which no work of any kind is permitted on the cars — no design, no manufacturing, no testing. The FIA enforces this through **access-control systems** at team factories that track who enters and exits, and teams are required to keep records of any activity during the period that can be audited later. The shutdown arrives at the rough midpoint of the 2026 season, which has so far produced wins for Lewis Hamilton (Barcelona), George Russell (Austria), Lando Norris (Hungary) and Kimi Antonelli (Belgium) — a spread that reflects an unusually competitive season. Racing resumes with the **Dutch Grand Prix** at Zandvoort in August.
key_points: Starting **today, July 31**, all F1 teams enter a mandatory **two-week factory shutdown**.
Teams are **banned from working on their cars** at all during this period — it's a rare, enforced pause in a sport that runs nearly non-stop.
The FIA can check who enters and exits team factories via **access-control systems**, and teams must log any activity during the shutdown.
The break falls at the season's approximate halfway point, after a first half headlined by wins for **Lewis Hamilton, George Russell, Lando Norris, and Kimi Antonelli**.
Racing resumes with the **Dutch Grand Prix** at Zandvoort in August.

depth.background: F1's **mandatory summer shutdown** is a rule the sport introduced years ago as a cost-control and driver/staff welfare measure — with development budgets and team headcounts having ballooned, forcing every team to fully down tools for a set period stops the wealthiest teams from simply out-working smaller rivals during the sport's only real off-week. The rule is strictly enforced: teams must log all facility activity during the shutdown, and the **FIA**, the sport's governing body, can request those logs and cross-check them against electronic access records at any time.

stories.title: The rupee is under pressure again as rising US bond yields squeeze the RBI's options
stories.what_happened: The Indian rupee weakened to around **95.55 per US dollar** on July 31, pressured by a rise in US Treasury yields that is pulling global investment money toward dollar assets. The RBI has been intervening by **selling dollars from its reserves on a near-daily basis**, which has helped the rupee claw back more than 1% after a sharper earlier slide toward record lows. Separately, at its most recent policy meeting, the RBI **held its repo rate steady at 5.25%** for the second consecutive time, maintaining a neutral policy stance instead of cutting rates to support growth. The central bank kept its FY27 growth forecast at **6.6%**, while flagging that elevated oil prices and an uneven monsoon — which has delayed sowing of key crops — could weigh on the outlook.
key_points: The **rupee (USD/INR)** touched **95.55**, edging toward record-low territory, as US bond yields climb.
The **RBI has been selling dollars daily** to slow the rupee's fall, an intervention that's already helped it recover **over 1%** from its worst levels.
The RBI held its **repo rate at 5.25%** for a second straight meeting, keeping a 'neutral' stance rather than cutting.
The central bank still expects **6.6% GDP growth** for FY27, but flags **elevated oil prices** and a **patchy monsoon** as risks.
If US yields keep rising, the RBI may be forced to **keep rates higher for longer** than it would otherwise want.

depth.background: The **rupee's exchange rate** is shaped by how attractive Indian assets are to foreign investors relative to alternatives like US Treasury bonds. When **US bond yields** (the return investors get from US government debt) rise, it becomes more attractive to hold dollars instead of rupees, pushing the rupee down. A weaker rupee makes imports — especially oil, which India buys almost entirely from abroad — more expensive, which can push up inflation. The **RBI (Reserve Bank of India)** manages this partly by directly buying or selling dollars in the market, and partly through its interest-rate decisions.

stories.title: Supreme Court refuses to cancel bail for Haldwani riots 'mastermind' Abdul Malik, questions why an anti-terror law was even used
stories.what_happened: The Supreme Court, in a bench comprising **Chief Justice Surya Kant** and Justices **Joymalya Bagchi** and **V. Mohan**, refused to interfere with the Uttarakhand High Court's decision to grant bail to Malik, rejecting the state government's appeal to have that bail cancelled. The bench noted that the ongoing investigation itself indicated Malik was **not present at the scene** when the violence occurred, undercutting the case for keeping him in custody. Justice Bagchi went further, openly questioning the state's use of UAPA in the case, asking how the law — designed for terrorism and organized unlawful activity — could apply simply because a mob attacked a police station. The court told the state's counsel it should focus on winning a conviction at trial rather than continuing to fight the bail decision, and noted that bail orders, even if imperfectly worded, don't need to be revisited over technical wording issues.
key_points: The **Supreme Court** dismissed the **Uttarakhand government's** appeal seeking to cancel bail granted to **Abdul Malik**, accused as the 'mastermind' of the **2024 Haldwani (Banbhoolpura) violence**.
A bench led by **Chief Justice of India Surya Kant**, with Justices **Joymalya Bagchi** and **V. Mohan**, upheld the Uttarakhand High Court's **April 16, 2026** bail order.
Justice Bagchi pointedly asked: **"Even if a mob goes and throws petrol bombs at a police station, how is UAPA attracted?"** — questioning the use of the anti-terror **UAPA law**.
The High Court had granted bail partly because the **investigation itself showed Malik was not present** at the scene during the violence.
The bench told the state's lawyers to **"focus your energy on securing a conviction rather than challenging the grant of bail."**

depth.background: The case dates back to **February 8, 2024**, when violence broke out in the **Banbhoolpura** area of **Haldwani**, Uttarakhand, after authorities moved to demolish an allegedly illegal religious structure; a mob reportedly attacked a police station during the unrest. Malik was accused of masterminding the violence and charged under the **Indian Penal Code**, the **Arms Act**, and the **Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA)** — India's principal anti-terrorism law, which carries much tougher bail conditions than ordinary criminal charges. The case has since become a test of how broadly Indian courts will allow UAPA to be applied to riot and mob-violence cases rather than reserving it for organized terrorism.

stories.title: Scientists find two never-before-seen 'ghost' human ancestors hidden in our DNA
stories.what_happened: A research team published a new technique in the journal **Science** that compares genealogical patterns across more than **500 present-day human genomes** to detect ancient interbreeding events that left no fossils behind. Using it, they identified two entirely new extinct lineages. The first, dubbed a **'ghost ancestor,'** split from the ancestors of modern humans about **800,000 years ago** and interbred with early humans in Africa more than **50,000 years ago** — its DNA now makes up roughly **0.5-1% of every person's genome**. The second, a **'super-archaic' population**, split off even earlier, around **1.8 million years ago**, and never interbred directly with modern humans — instead it mixed with Denisovans in Eurasia, who then passed a small trace of that ancient DNA on to us. Neither lineage has ever been found as a fossil.
key_points: A new genome-scanning technique found **two previously unknown extinct human lineages** buried in modern DNA.
One 'ghost' population split off **800,000 years ago** and later interbred with early humans in Africa **50,000+ years ago**.
A second, 'super-archaic' lineage split **1.8 million years ago** and passed DNA to us indirectly, via the Denisovans.
Every person alive today carries **0.5% to 1%** of their genome from the African ghost lineage.
The method scanned **500+ modern human genomes** worldwide, rather than relying on rare fossil DNA.

depth.background: Scientists have known for over a decade that modern humans aren't a single, pure lineage — we carry small amounts of DNA from **Neanderthals** and **Denisovans**, two extinct human relatives who interbred with our ancestors tens of thousands of years ago. But fossil DNA is rare and degrades over time, so entire branches of the human family tree could exist with no physical trace at all. Researchers have long suspected 'ghost lineages' — populations we can only detect indirectly, through the genetic fingerprints they left in living people.

stories.title: Verstappen tells Red Bull its 'big priority' is raw pace, not fixing the RB22's mid-race dropoffs
stories.what_happened: Heading into F1's summer shutdown, Max Verstappen described the season's first half as **'very tough,'** having managed four podiums but **no wins** across 11 races and sitting fourth in the drivers' standings. He said Red Bull's priority for the second half must be **finding more raw overall performance** in the RB22, and separately fixing a specific problem where the car **loses performance over the course of a race weekend, or even from the start of a race to the end**. Team principal Laurent Mekies acknowledged the team may soon have to scale back development of the current car to protect resources for the 2027 regulation reset, while former team advisor Helmut Marko said he doesn't think Red Bull can repeat the kind of second-half turnaround it pulled off in 2025.
key_points: Verstappen enters the summer break **winless** for the first time in years, sitting **fourth** in the standings.
He says Red Bull's top priority must be finding **more overall performance**, not just fixing inconsistency.
The RB22 sometimes **loses performance mid-race**, from the start of a race to its end.
Team boss Laurent Mekies admits Red Bull may soon have to **cut development** of this year's car to focus on 2027.
Former Red Bull advisor Helmut Marko doubts the team can repeat last year's second-half comeback.

depth.background: Red Bull built its recent championship dominance around Max Verstappen, but a shift in F1's technical rules for 2026 reset the competitive order, and Red Bull's **RB22** has struggled to match the pace of rivals like McLaren, Mercedes and Ferrari through the season's first 11 rounds. Verstappen's contract reportedly contains performance-linked exit clauses that could let him leave if the team keeps underperforming, adding pressure on Red Bull to turn the car around before too much of the season slips away.

stories.title: Trump orders a new wave of strikes on Iran aimed at forcing surrender, as US tells citizens to be ready to leave the Middle East
stories.what_happened: The Wall Street Journal, citing unnamed US officials, reported that President Trump has ordered a new wave of military strikes on Iran, explicitly aimed at forcing the Islamic Republic's surrender. The bombing campaign could begin **as soon as this weekend** and is expected to last several days. CBS reported the US is weighing strikes on Iran's **oil refineries and power plants** — a shift from hitting only military and nuclear sites to targeting the civilian economy directly. In response, **US embassies in Israel, Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Egypt** issued advisories urging American citizens to consider leaving the region or be ready to depart if the situation escalates. Trump told reporters 'we'll be hitting them very hard,' adding that at some point Iran will say it 'can't take it anymore.' The move follows the breakdown of nuclear negotiations and comes after Iran fired missiles at a US base that American defenses intercepted.
key_points: The Wall Street Journal reports Trump has **ordered fresh US strikes on Iran**, which could begin as soon as this weekend.
Targets reportedly include Iran's **power stations and oil refineries** — civilian energy infrastructure, not just military sites.
US embassies across **12 Middle East countries** urged American citizens to consider leaving or prepare to depart.
Trump publicly said the US will hit Iran '**very hard**,' predicting Tehran will eventually say it 'can't take it anymore.'
The order follows the **collapse of nuclear talks** and an Iranian missile attack on a US base that was intercepted.

depth.background: Israel and the US have been at war with Iran on and off for months, and the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway that a fifth of the world's oil passes through — has already effectively shut down after Iran started intercepting tankers. As recently as yesterday, US and Israeli officials were reportedly **still weighing** a joint strike on Iran's energy infrastructure, with no final decision made and Trump not yet having given the order. That changed within a day: multiple outlets, citing the **Wall Street Journal**, now report Trump has actually issued the order.

stories.title: Lok Sabha passes a births-and-deaths registration bill 'without discussion' as opposition uproar over a student crackdown paralyses Parliament
stories.what_happened: Amid continuing opposition protests over the July 20 police crackdown on student demonstrators, the Lok Sabha passed the **Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026** by voice vote, with no meaningful debate as opposition MPs shouted slogans in the well of the House. The bill tightens rules for late registration of births and deaths: a report filed **one to two years late** now needs approval from a District or Sub-Divisional Magistrate after verification, while anything registered **more than two years late** requires an order from a judicial magistrate. Separately, Congress MPs moved adjournment motions in both Houses seeking a discussion on what they call the 'disproportionate and excessive' use of force — including lathi-charges, tear gas, pellet guns and shock batons — against students during the July 20 march, citing specific injuries including a protester who allegedly suffered serious eye injuries from pellets. The Rajya Sabha has been adjourned until August 3 as the impasse continues.
key_points: The **Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026** was passed by the Lok Sabha by voice vote, amid ruckus and with no debate.
The bill makes registering a birth or death **more than a year late** require magistrate approval, and **beyond two years** require a judicial magistrate's order.
Opposition MPs are demanding Home Minister Amit Shah answer for **police action against student protesters** on July 20.
Protesters allege **lathi-charges, tear gas and pellet guns** were used, with some student injuries described as severe.
The Rajya Sabha has been **adjourned until August 3** as the standoff continues.

depth.background: On July 20, thousands of students marched on Parliament in a 'Chalo Sansad' protest demanding accountability over the NEET-UG medical entrance exam paper leak. Delhi Police and Rapid Action Force personnel used force to disperse the crowd, and the opposition — led by Congress — says the response was disproportionate, citing named students who suffered serious injuries. Since Parliament's monsoon session resumed, opposition MPs have repeatedly disrupted proceedings demanding Home Minister Amit Shah explain the police action and that criminal cases against protesting students be withdrawn.

stories.title: Bank of Japan holds rates at a 30-year high and warns inflation will blow past its target
stories.what_happened: The Bank of Japan kept its short-term policy rate unchanged at **1.0%** at its July 2026 meeting, the highest level since September 1995, in a widely expected **8-1 vote**. Board member Hajime Takata dissented, arguing for an immediate hike to 1.25%. In its quarterly outlook, the BOJ said core inflation — prices excluding volatile food costs — is on track to climb **'clearly above' its 2% target** starting in the second half of the fiscal year, which begins in September. The bank actually trimmed its FY2026 inflation forecast slightly, to 2.5% from 2.8%, citing government steps to ease households' summer energy bills, even though July's core inflation reading itself came in at 1.6%, still below target. Officials pointed to rising wages feeding into retail prices, elevated crude oil costs, and a weaker yen as the key forces pushing prices up later this year.
key_points: The BOJ held its policy rate at **1.0%**, the **highest level since 1995**, after an 8-1 vote.
One board member dissented, pushing for a hike to **1.25%** instead.
The bank now expects core inflation to run **'clearly above' its 2% target** from this September.
It trimmed its FY2026 inflation forecast slightly to **2.5%** after government energy-cost relief.
A weaker **yen**, rising wages, and high crude oil costs are all pushing prices higher.

depth.background: Japan spent decades battling the opposite problem — **deflation**, or falling prices, which discourages spending and investment because people expect things to get cheaper if they wait. The Bank of Japan (BOJ) kept interest rates near zero or negative for most of that time to try to force prices up. That era ended as inflation returned globally after 2022, and the BOJ has been cautiously raising rates ever since, most recently lifting them from 0.75% to 1% in June 2026. Japan's central bank sets policy through its Policy Board, and a public dissent from a board member — as happened this time — signals that some officials think the bank is moving too slowly.

stories.title: Parliament makes disrespecting Vande Mataram a crime, on par with the National Anthem
stories.what_happened: Parliament passed the **Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026**, extending to Vande Mataram the same legal shield that already covers the National Anthem, the National Flag, and the Constitution. The **Lok Sabha passed it on July 30**, and the **Rajya Sabha followed a day later**, both by voice vote, clearing its final parliamentary hurdle before it goes to **President Droupadi Murmu** for assent to become law. Under the new law, anyone who intentionally insults Vande Mataram, or deliberately stops an assembly from singing it, faces **up to three years in prison**, a fine, or both — mirroring the penalty that already applies to disrespecting the National Anthem. The bill's timing lines up with a year-long official commemoration of **'150 years of Vande Mataram'**, running from November 2025 to November 2026, marking the song's 1875 origin. During debate, BJP lawmakers framed the song as a unifying symbol that inspired independence-era freedom fighters, while opposition MPs — including DMK's **Kanimozhi** — argued the move risked stoking division rather than easing it.
key_points: Parliament passed a bill giving **Vande Mataram** the same legal protection as the **National Anthem**.
Insulting it can now mean **up to 3 years in prison**, a fine, or both.
The **Lok Sabha passed it July 30**, the **Rajya Sabha a day later**, both by voice vote.
It's timed to a year-long **'150 years of Vande Mataram'** commemoration running to November 2026.
Opposition MPs like DMK's **Kanimozhi** warned it could deepen social division, not unity.

depth.background: **Vande Mataram** ('I bow to thee, Mother') is India's official National Song, written by Bengali writer Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay in 1875 and later adopted as a rallying cry during India's freedom struggle against British rule. It sits alongside — but distinct from — the National Anthem, 'Jana Gana Mana,' which already carries criminal penalties for disrespect under a 1971 law. The song has long been a sensitive topic for some religious minority communities because of imagery in its full version that some read as tied to Hindu nationalist symbolism, so debates over legally protecting it have surfaced periodically for decades.

stories.title: England cricket boss Rob Key defends Andrew Flintoff against 'disrespectful' criticism
stories.what_happened: Rob Key launched a strong public defense of Andrew Flintoff after criticism of his Lions coaching role, including a Sunday Times piece calling the arrangement a 'serious error.' Key called the criticism 'unfair' and 'disrespectful,' describing Flintoff as an 'unsung hero' of the English cricket system who has done the Lions job for several years despite being able to earn significantly more money elsewhere. Key also defended the England and Wales Cricket Board's (**ECB**) decision to let Flintoff leave an upcoming England Lions tour of South Africa early so he can take a paid coaching role with **Sydney Thunder** in Australia's Big Bash League T20 competition.
key_points: England men's cricket director **Rob Key** defended **Andrew Flintoff** against media criticism.
The Sunday Times had called Flintoff's Lions coaching role a **'serious error.'**
Key called Flintoff an **'unsung hero'** who could earn far more money elsewhere.
Flintoff will leave an England Lions tour early for a **Big Bash League** coaching job in Australia.

depth.background: **Andrew Flintoff** ('Freddie') is one of England's most celebrated former all-rounders, part of the team that won the famous 2005 Ashes series. He has coached the **England Lions**, the country's development/A team that grooms future senior players and coaches, since September 2024, and re-signed through 2027. He's been floated repeatedly as a possible future senior England head coach but has said he doesn't want that job. **Rob Key** is England men's cricket managing director, the top administrative role overseeing team and coaching decisions.

stories.title: Sky Sports' David Croft calls out Lewis Hamilton's season of 'careless' penalties
stories.what_happened: Sky Sports F1's lead commentator **David Croft** criticized Hamilton on the Sky Sports F1 Show for a pattern of avoidable penalties running through the 2026 season: a pit-lane speeding penalty at Monaco, a jump-start penalty at Silverstone, a collision penalty with **George Russell** at Spa, a grid penalty for impeding Piastri in qualifying, and most recently a pit-lane speeding penalty at the Hungarian Grand Prix. On that last one, Croft revealed Hamilton released his pit-lane speed limiter about **five metres too early** while racing title rival **Kimi Antonelli** to the safety-car line for position — enough to breach the speed limit by just 0.1 km/h. 'You can't throw away positions by making these sort of mistakes,' Croft said. 'I don't want to go too hard on Lewis – I think he's the greatest of all time – but these are not moments that a driver of his ability and experience should be making.' Hamilton finished the Hungarian GP in 5th after picking up two separate penalties that race weekend.
key_points: Commentator **David Croft** publicly criticized Hamilton for a season-long run of avoidable penalties.
Croft listed five separate penalties this season, from **Monaco to Hungary**.
At Hungary, Hamilton broke the pit-lane speed limit by just **0.1 km/h**, racing Antonelli for position.
Croft still called Hamilton **'the greatest of all time'** despite the criticism.
Hamilton finished the Hungarian GP 5th after picking up **two separate penalties** that weekend.

depth.background: **Lewis Hamilton**, a seven-time world champion, moved to **Ferrari** for the 2025 season in one of the biggest driver transfers in F1 history, but his first two seasons there have been rockier than expected as he adapts to a new car and team. Pit-lane speed limits are strict-liability rules — even a fractional breach, regardless of intent, triggers an automatic time penalty — which is why a margin as small as 0.1 km/h can still cost a driver track position.

stories.title: McLaren steals a jump on rivals testing at Portimão, a track now in the running to host F1's season finale
stories.what_happened: McLaren ran a two-day TPC test at Portimão on **July 29-30**, using the older-spec MCL60 car shared between championship leader **Lando Norris**, his teammate **Oscar Piastri**, and McLaren reserve/F2 driver **Leonardo Fornaroli**. On the final day alone the trio combined for **151 laps**: Norris ran 49 laps, Piastri 55, and Fornaroli 47. The test had been booked well before Portimão became a live topic on the 2026 calendar, but it's taken on extra significance now that Portimão has emerged as a leading candidate to replace Qatar and/or Abu Dhabi as the season finale, given growing doubts those Middle East races can safely go ahead. Because McLaren got laps in before any rival team, it now holds an edge in setup and tyre correlation data if the race there is confirmed.
key_points: McLaren ran a **two-day test** at Portimão, Portugal with Norris, Piastri and reserve **Leonardo Fornaroli**.
The trio combined for **151 laps** on the final day using an older-spec MCL60 car.

depth.background: F1 teams are allowed limited 'Testing of Previous Cars' (TPC) sessions using older-spec cars, separate from official pre-season testing, mainly for driver practice, tyre development and sponsor commitments. Portimão's Autódromo Internacional do Algarve hosted F1 races in 2020-21 during COVID-era schedule gaps but hasn't held a round since. F1's traditional season-ending races, Qatar and Abu Dhabi, have come into doubt this year because of the deteriorating security situation across the Middle East, pushing organizers to quietly explore backup venues.

stories.title: Russia hammers Ukraine with 255 drones overnight, killing 9, as strikes stretch into a fourth straight night
stories.what_happened: Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 255 drones overnight into July 31 — a combination of **Shahed-type attack drones** (some jet-powered for extra speed), Gerbera and Italmas drones, and Parodiya decoys meant to confuse air defences and burn through interceptor missiles. Ukrainian air defences shot down or neutralized 195 of the drones, but the remainder still struck 14 locations, with debris from downed drones falling at four more sites. Local authorities said the attacks over the past day killed 9 people and injured 48 across the country, coming just a day after a separate mass strike killed at least 8 and wounded more than 50. This marks the fourth consecutive night of large-scale Russian aerial attacks on Ukraine.
key_points: Russia launched **255 attack and decoy drones** at Ukraine overnight — a mix of Shahed, Gerbera and Italmas types plus Parodiya decoys.
Ukrainian air defences destroyed **195 of them**, but strikes still landed at **14 separate locations**.
The attack killed **9 people and injured 48** over the past day, local officials said.

This is now the **fourth straight night** of large-scale Russian strikes on Ukraine.

depth.background: Russia has been running sustained, near-nightly bombardments of Ukrainian cities using cheap, mass-produced Shahed-type drones alongside cruise and ballistic missiles — a tactic designed to overwhelm Ukraine's more expensive air-defence systems through sheer volume. Two nights ago, a similar mass attack killed at least 8 people, and a stray missile briefly crossed into Poland, forcing NATO to scramble fighter jets — a reminder that these strikes carry risk of spilling beyond Ukraine's borders. Kyiv and other cities have now endured repeated nights of this pattern with little sign of let-up.

stories.title: US and Israel line up joint weekend strikes on Iran's power stations and oil refineries
stories.what_happened: Multiple US outlets, citing officials familiar with the planning, reported that the United States and Israel are preparing to bombard Iranian energy-related targets, potentially starting as soon as this weekend. The expected target list includes **power stations and oil refineries** — infrastructure that would hit Iran's economy and civilian energy supply, not just its military. Officials say Israel has been briefed and is coordinating with Washington, and a joint strike would represent Israel's re-entry into direct combat operations against Iran. There was internal discussion about finishing any campaign **before US and global markets open on Monday**, reflecting concern about the economic shockwaves a prolonged bombing campaign could send through oil markets. Crucially, multiple reports stress that **no final decision has been made** — President Trump has not issued the order to proceed, and the timeline could still slip or be called off.
key_points: US and Israeli officials are preparing what could be **the harshest bombing campaign yet** on Iran's energy infrastructure, sources say.
Targets reportedly include **power stations and oil refineries**, not just military sites.
Planners are weighing wrapping up strikes **before financial markets open Monday**, worried about the economic fallout.
It would mark **Israel's return to combat** against Iran after sitting out during the US-brokered truce.
**Trump has not given a final 'go' order** — officials stress no decision is locked in yet.

depth.background: Ten days ago, the US struck targets inside Iran, and Iran retaliated by hitting Kuwait and Jordan, killing one person — the exchange that first pulled the Gulf states into this round of the conflict. Since then, a fragile calm has held, but Washington and Israel have kept the option of further strikes on the table, this time aimed at the economic backbone of Iran's regime — its **energy infrastructure** — rather than just military or nuclear sites. Israel had stepped back from active strikes during the US-brokered truce; officials say a joint operation now would effectively end that pause.

thread.previously: Iran struck Kuwait and Jordan, killing one person, hours after the US had hit targets inside Iran — the exchange that opened this latest round of the conflict.

stories.title: The rupee claws back to a near three-week high after the RBI sells $7 billion to defend it
stories.what_happened: The rupee strengthened to around 95.67 per dollar, extending its gains for a fourth straight session to reach its strongest level in nearly three weeks, according to currency market reports. The move was driven by the US dollar's biggest slide in three months and a modest pullback in oil prices, combined with sustained, aggressive intervention by the **Reserve Bank of India**, which has continued selling dollars from its reserves to support the currency. The rupee is up about 0.9% for the week, on track for its best weekly showing in four months. This marks a notable reversal from earlier concern that the rupee was under renewed pressure as rising US bond yields squeezed the RBI's options.
key_points: The rupee strengthened to around **95.67 per dollar**, its best level in nearly **three weeks**.
It was the currency's **fourth straight session of gains**, its best run in four months.
The **Reserve Bank of India sold about $7 billion** in a single session earlier to stop an earlier slide.
A **pullback in oil prices** and the **dollar's biggest slide in three months** also helped the rupee.
The rupee had touched a **record low near 96.84** to the dollar earlier this year before this recovery.

depth.background: The rupee had been sliding toward record lows earlier this year, squeezed by elevated oil prices, US tariff moves, and rising US bond yields that pulled money out of emerging markets like India and toward the US dollar. A weak rupee makes everything India imports — from oil to electronics — more expensive, feeding inflation, and the RBI's playbook for defending the currency is to sell dollars from its foreign-exchange reserves to soak up demand for the greenback. It intervened aggressively before, at one point reportedly selling around $7 billion in a single day to defend the currency near its record low.

stories.title: Modi's Cabinet clears ₹5,070 crore scheme to float solar panels on India's reservoirs
stories.what_happened: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved the 'Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana (PM-SSY)' on July 31, a scheme to build floating solar photovoltaic projects paired with **energy storage systems** on reservoirs and industrial ponds. The plan targets **5,000 MW of capacity**, with the government offering **central financial assistance of ₹1 crore per MW** to developers once projects are commissioned, plus additional support for feasibility studies. The total outlay is **₹5,070 crore**, with projects to be sanctioned between FY2026-27 and FY2030-31 and financial support disbursed through FY2032-33. The government projects the scheme will cut CO₂ emissions by roughly 10 million tonnes annually, generate 16,000-17,000 jobs, and boost domestic manufacturing of solar components in line with its 'Aatmanirbhar Bharat' (self-reliant India) push.
key_points: The new **'PM Surya Sarovar Yojana'** targets **5,000 MW** of floating solar power with attached battery storage.
The government will pay developers **₹1 crore (about $120,000) per MW** in support once projects are commissioned.
Projects run from **FY2026-27 to FY2030-31**, with payouts continuing through FY2032-33.
The scheme is expected to **cut CO₂ emissions by 10 million tonnes a year** and create **16,000-17,000 jobs**.
It uses **reservoirs and industrial ponds** instead of land, sidestepping India's land-acquisition bottleneck for new solar.

depth.background: India has been racing to add renewable power capacity to meet both its climate targets and surging electricity demand, but large ground-mounted solar farms often get stuck in slow, contentious **land acquisition** — buying up or leasing the land needed to build them. Floating solar — panels mounted on rafts over reservoirs, canals or industrial ponds — sidesteps that problem entirely and has the added benefit of reducing water evaporation from the reservoir underneath. The scheme was cleared at the same Union Cabinet meeting on July 31 that also approved a large offshore oil-and-gas exploration push and an extension of the country's main farmer income-support scheme, underlining a broader push to lock in big-ticket infrastructure and welfare spending ahead of the 2026-27 fiscal year.

stories.title: Hardik Pandya trade war escalates as CSK and Mumbai Indians haggle over a two-for-one deal

Kolkata Knight Riders and Rajasthan Royals have also reportedly made contact with MI management to gauge interest in adding Pandya. stories.title: Australia Women thrash India Women to seal the ODI series, Georgia Voll's century the difference
stories.what_happened: Australia Women beat India Women by 5 wickets in the second ODI at Bellerive Oval in Hobart, chasing down India's total of 251/9 with 252/5 in 36.1 overs — well inside their 50-over allocation. India's total was built around a 54 from captain **Harmanpreet Kaur** and 52 from **Pratika Rawal**. In reply, Australia's chase was powered by a **century from Georgia Voll** and 80 from Phoebe Litchfield, who between them did most of the scoring work. The result gives Australia the two-match ODI leg of the tour 2-0, and lifts them to a 6-4 points lead in the overall multi-format series, which still has the ODI series finale and a one-off Test in Perth remaining.

stories.title: Carlos Sainz signals he's staying at Williams as Audi's door quietly closes

stories.title: IBM and Sarvam team up to build 'sovereign AI' for India's government and regulated industries
stories.what_happened: IBM and Sarvam announced on **July 31, 2026** a collaboration to advance 'full-stack AI sovereignty' for government agencies, public-sector organizations, and regulated enterprises across India. The partnership pairs **IBM Sovereign Core** — IBM's sovereign-by-design software giving customers full control over data, operations, and governance — with **Sarvam's Sovereign AI stack**, which includes reasoning models and India-first language and voice AI trained from scratch domestically. The two companies will jointly pilot use cases such as **citizen services, grievance redressal, document processing, and administrative workflows**. The **IBM GovTech AI Innovation Center in Lucknow** will act as the joint hub where government departments and enterprises can work through the technical and governance requirements of moving AI pilots into real production use.
key_points: IBM and Indian AI startup **Sarvam** announced a partnership on **July 31** to build 'sovereign AI' for Indian government and regulated enterprises.

depth.background: 'Sovereign AI' means a country or organization keeps control of the data, infrastructure, and governance behind its AI systems, instead of depending on foreign-owned cloud platforms — a growing concern for governments handling sensitive citizen data. **Sarvam AI** is one of India's homegrown AI labs, building models trained specifically on Indian languages and use cases, part of a broader push (alongside efforts like BharatGen) to reduce India's reliance on US and Chinese AI providers for public-sector deployments.

stories.title: Maruti Suzuki's profit falls 9% even as revenue jumps 36%, on India's biggest earnings day of the season
stories.what_happened: Maruti Suzuki reported **Q1 FY27** results on **July 31**: consolidated net profit fell **9.11%** year-on-year to **₹3,446.9 crore**, down from ₹3,792.4 crore a year earlier, even though revenue from operations jumped **35.9%** to ₹52,469.8 crore. Maruti reported alongside more than 100 other Indian companies the same day, including ITC, Sun Pharma, Indian Oil, Bajaj Finserv, GAIL, and Dixon Technologies.

Automakers globally have faced a mix of strong demand but rising input costs this year, partly linked to the West Asia conflict pushing up commodity and shipping costs.

stories.title: Namibia chase down Netherlands to boost their 2027 World Cup qualifying hopes
stories.what_happened: In the **120th match** of the ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2 at Sportpark Maarschalkerweerd in **Utrecht** on **July 31**, Namibia chased down the Netherlands' total of **183** with **186 for 4 in 41 overs**, winning by **6 wickets** with 54 balls to spare. **Jan Frylinck** anchored the chase with **68 runs off 75 balls** and was named Player of the Match. The win comes just days after the Netherlands beat Namibia by 58 runs in an earlier meeting between the two sides in the same series.
key_points: Namibia beat the Netherlands by **6 wickets**, chasing 183 with **186/4** in 41 overs at Utrecht.
**Jan Frylinck** was Player of the Match with **68 runs off 75 balls**.
The result matters for **2027 Cricket World Cup qualification** — the top four in League 2 advance directly, the rest face a Qualifier Play-off.
It was the **120th match** of the ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2, a multi-year league among associate nations.

depth.background: The **ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2** is a multi-year one-day international league among cricket's 'associate' nations — countries like Netherlands, Namibia, Nepal, USA and others outside the sport's traditional Test-playing top tier — competing for World Cup qualification spots. Namibia, best known globally for reaching the Super 12 stage of the T20 World Cup in 2021 and 2022, has been battling in the middle of the League 2 table, needing wins like this to stay in contention for a top-four finish that guarantees a route to the 2027 ODI World Cup Qualifier.

stories.title: Oscar Piastri heads into F1's summer break 36 points behind his own teammate after a costly Hungarian GP
stories.what_happened: At the **Hungarian Grand Prix on July 26**, Lando Norris converted pole position into his first full victory of the 2026 season, snapping a lengthy drought, after early leader and teammate Oscar Piastri lost time following a collision with Carlos Sainz and then retired entirely with a **gearbox failure**. That result swung the intra-McLaren battle sharply: Piastri dropped to seventh in the standings on 92 points, now **36 points behind** Norris's 128. Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli, who finished on the podium in Hungary, heads into the break with roughly a **50-point championship lead** over the rest of the field. Formula 1 then entered its mandatory **two-week summer shutdown** starting today, July 31, during which teams' factories close and no work on the cars is permitted.
key_points: Oscar Piastri now sits **36 points** behind McLaren teammate Lando Norris heading into F1's summer break, after retiring from the Hungarian GP with a **gearbox failure**.
Norris broke a **long win drought**, taking his first full-race victory of the season at the Hungaroring on July 26.
Mercedes rookie **Kimi Antonelli** leads the overall championship by roughly **50 points** after Hungary.
F1 enters a mandatory **two-week shutdown** starting today, July 31 — teams are barred from touching their cars until it ends.

depth.background: Formula 1's summer break is a mandated mid-season pause — teams' factories must fully close for a set period and no one is allowed to work on the cars, giving everyone a breather roughly halfway through the season. Heading into the break, **Kimi Antonelli**, Mercedes' teenage title contender, has been the season's most consistent performer, while McLaren teammates **Lando Norris** and **Oscar Piastri** have been fighting a title battle of their own inside the same team.

stories.title: Jasprit Bumrah passes his fitness tests and is cleared to play India's Sri Lanka Test series
stories.what_happened: Multiple reports now say Bumrah has **completed the fitness tests mandated by the BCCI's Centre of Excellence** and been **cleared to play** India's upcoming two-Test series in Sri Lanka. A senior BCCI official confirmed he is expected to be available for both matches. The series' first Test starts **August 15 in Galle**, with the second in **Colombo from August 23**, both part of the ongoing World Test Championship cycle. His return comes as India has been managing several other injury concerns — Washington Sundar, Harshit Rana and Nitish Reddy are all out — making Bumrah's clearance a significant boost. The **August 7 practice match** in Colombo, previously flagged as the definitive checkpoint, still appears likely to serve as a further workload gauge before the first Test.
key_points: **Jasprit Bumrah** has completed all fitness tests mandated by the **BCCI's Centre of Excellence** in Bengaluru.
He is now expected to be **available for both Tests** against Sri Lanka, per a senior BCCI official.
He had been sidelined by a **torn left knee ligament** suffered in the 2nd ODI against England at Cardiff.
The two-Test series starts **August 15 in Galle**, with the second Test in **Colombo from August 23**.
A practice match in Colombo on **August 7** still stands as a further workload checkpoint before the series.

depth.background: Bumrah, India's premier fast bowler, tore a ligament in his left knee during a collision in the **2nd ODI against England at Cardiff**, an injury that forced him out of the series-deciding third ODI at Lord's. He'd been in a structured rehab program since, with his scheduled rest period ending on **July 30**, when he reported to the BCCI's Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru for the next phase of fitness assessment. India had already named him in a 15-man squad for the Sri Lanka tour, but only **conditional on clearing fitness** — with a practice match in Colombo on August 7 flagged by selectors as the real deciding checkpoint.

thread.previously: Bumrah's rest period for a torn left knee ligament ended on July 30, when he reported to the BCCI's Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru for the next phase of fitness assessment; a practice match in Colombo on August 7 was flagged as the real deciding checkpoint for his availability.
thread.changed: He has now completed the fitness tests mandated by the Centre of Excellence and been cleared by the BCCI to play both Tests against Sri Lanka, according to a senior BCCI official — though the August 7 practice match still appears likely to serve as a further workload check.

stories.title: F1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli sued by his former manager just as the summer break begins
stories.what_happened: Giovanni Minardi has filed a civil lawsuit against Kimi Antonelli in the **Court of Bologna**, alleging **unpaid compensation** after Antonelli **unilaterally terminated their management agreement** before making his Formula 1 debut. The management relationship dated back to when Antonelli was just eight years old and competing in karting. According to reports, the amount in dispute runs into **six figures**, and the two parties are reportedly **not close to reaching a settlement**. The suit surfaces just as Formula 1 enters its mandatory two-week **summer factory shutdown**, meaning Antonelli will be dealing with the legal matter during what's normally downtime from racing.
key_points: **Kimi Antonelli**, Mercedes' 2026 championship leader, is being **sued by his former manager**, Giovanni Minardi.
The lawsuit was filed in the **Court of Bologna**, Italy, over allegedly **unpaid compensation**.
Minardi is the son of **Giancarlo Minardi**, founder of the old Minardi F1 team.
Antonelli joined Minardi Management as an **8-year-old karter**, before later moving to Mercedes' junior program.
The dispute reportedly involves a **six-figure sum**, and the two sides are **not close to settling**.

depth.background: **Kimi Antonelli** is F1's breakout story of 2026 — a teenager leading the drivers' championship and on pace to become the sport's youngest-ever world champion, currently around **50 points clear of Lewis Hamilton**. Before he ever reached Formula 1, Antonelli was managed by **Giovanni Minardi**, whose father Giancarlo founded the historic (now defunct) Minardi F1 team, while Antonelli was still karting as a child. Ferrari passed on signing him at the time due to his young age, and he ultimately joined **Mercedes' junior driver program in 2018**, the pathway that led to his current seat.

stories.title: Trump says Hamas has agreed to disarm — but Israel and Hamas both stop short of confirming it
stories.what_happened: President Trump said Thursday that talks in Cairo had produced a deal for Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza to **fully disarm**, describing it as a historic breakthrough for his broader peace plan. He said the disarmament would happen **in phases** rather than all at once. But the announcement came with a catch: a Board of Peace official said the specific document on the table has Hamas placing its heavy weapons into **storage**, not destroying them — and an unnamed Israeli official said, just before Trump spoke, that Israel had rejected an earlier version of the proposal because it didn't guarantee weapons actually leave Gaza. Hamas's own written response, seen by Reuters, notably **did not say** whether it agrees to disarm and demilitarize. So as of today, the US side is describing a deal that the two parties who'd have to live with it haven't yet confirmed.
key_points: Trump announced a **'historic agreement'** for the complete disarmament of Hamas and all armed groups in Gaza, to happen **in phases**
**Neither Hamas nor Israel** has publicly confirmed accepting the deal Trump described
An Israeli official said before the announcement that Israel had **rejected** the proposal, demanding full demilitarization as a precondition
Under the plan, Hamas would **store** its heavy weapons rather than destroy them — a distinction critics call insufficient
A Board of Peace official estimated the process could take **200 to 320 days**

depth.background: The current Gaza ceasefire was signed roughly **nine months ago** under a US-brokered framework, ending the acute phase of the war but leaving the harder questions — who governs Gaza, who rebuilds it, and what happens to Hamas's weapons — for a second phase. Trump set up a body he calls the **'Board of Peace'** to oversee that second phase, and mediators from **Egypt, Qatar and Turkey** have been shuttling between Hamas and Israeli officials in Cairo to close the gap. Every previous attempt to get Hamas to give up its arsenal has stalled, because disarmament is existential for the group — it's the one thing that guarantees it still matters politically once the guns go quiet.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported that Cairo talks between Hamas and mediators had made 'rare progress' on phase two of the US-brokered Gaza peace plan, with Hamas said to be discussing handing over its heavy weapons if Israel withdrew and stopped strikes.
thread.changed: Trump has now gone further, publicly declaring a 'historic agreement' for Hamas's complete disarmament — but neither Hamas nor Israel has confirmed they've actually accepted it, and Israeli officials say the terms fall short of their demands.

stories.title: India's boxers guarantee their best-ever Commonwealth Games haul — six fight for gold today, ten medals already banked
stories.what_happened: Six Indian boxers — **Sakshi Chaudhary, Arundhati Choudhary, Sachin Siwach, Ankush Yadav, Narender Berwal and Jaismine Lamboria** — advanced to the semi-finals this week, joining four who'd already booked their spots earlier: **Lovlina Borgohain** (who got a bye), **Priya Ghanghas, Preeti Pawar** and **Jadumani Singh Mandengbam**. Because every Commonwealth Games boxing semi-finalist is guaranteed at least a bronze medal, that combination locks in **10 medals for India** — a new national record for the sport at this event, beating the 9 won at Gold Coast 2018. Today, all ten fight their semi-final bouts, each with a shot at upgrading their guaranteed bronze to silver or gold.
key_points: **Six Indian boxers** reached the semi-finals this week, guaranteeing India at least **10 boxing medals** at Glasgow 2026
That beats India's **previous best of 9 boxing medals**, set at Gold Coast 2018
**Lovlina Borgohain**, an Olympic medallist, is already through to the semis after a bye in the quarter-finals
Ten Indian boxers total contest semi-final bouts today, each already assured of at least a bronze

depth.background: Boxing has quietly become one of India's most reliable medal sports at multi-nation events like the Commonwealth Games, built on a pipeline of Olympic and Asian Games medallists training together in a well-funded national program. At Gold Coast 2018, India's boxing contingent won 9 medals — the previous high-water mark the team has been chasing ever since. This year's Glasgow Games squad includes Olympic medallist **Lovlina Borgohain**, alongside a mix of experienced campaigners and rising talent across the men's and women's divisions.

stories.title: Lok Sabha passes birth-and-death registration bill without debate as Parliament stays gridlocked over the July 20 student crackdown
stories.what_happened: On Friday, the Lok Sabha passed the **Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026** by voice vote, with Minister of State for Home Affairs Nityanand Rai piloting it — but with no actual debate, because Opposition members were occupied protesting in the Well of the House and demanding Home Minister Amit Shah answer for the July 20 crackdown on student protesters. The bill itself tightens the rules for **delayed registration**: if a birth or death is reported more than two years after it happened, a magistrate must now approve the registration, rather than it being a routine bureaucratic process. With this bill through and the earlier anti-paper-leak bill passed a day earlier under similar walkout conditions, both Houses of Parliament have now been adjourned until **August 3**.
key_points: Lok Sabha passed the **Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026** by voice vote with zero debate
Opposition MPs trooped into the **Well of the House**, demanding Home Minister **Amit Shah** appear over the July 20 crackdown
The bill requires **judicial (magistrate) approval** for any birth/death registration filed **more than two years late**
Both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha have now been **adjourned until August 3**, extending the Monsoon Session logjam

depth.background: India's Monsoon Session of Parliament has been derailed for days by Opposition anger over a police crackdown on students during a **'Sansad Chalo' march to Parliament on July 20**, layered on top of ongoing anger over the **NEET (medical entrance exam) paper-leak scandal**. The government has been pushing through a backlog of routine legislation — bills that in a calmer session would get full floor debate — largely **unopposed procedurally but unheard substantively**, because Opposition MPs are boycotting debate and instead protesting in the Well of the House. This bill was cleared by the Union Cabinet on July 20, the same day as the crackdown that triggered the current standoff.

thread.previously: Yesterday, the Rajya Sabha passed the anti-paper-leak bill amid an opposition walkout, with MPs protesting both the NEET paper-leak scandal and a police crackdown on students during a Delhi march.
thread.changed: Today the standoff widened: the Lok Sabha passed a second, unrelated bill — on birth and death registration — by voice vote with **no debate at all**, as the Opposition kept up its protest over the July 20 crackdown, and both Houses have now been **adjourned till August 3**.

stories.title: Trump says he's 'not sure' he'll let Ukraine build Patriot missiles — a reversal from his own pledge three weeks ago
stories.what_happened: President Trump told reporters he is **'not sure'** whether the US will actually grant Ukraine a license to produce Patriot interceptor missiles, saying **'we're looking at it'** and that licensing such an **'extraordinary weapon'** requires caution. This walks back his own public commitment made at the NATO summit in Ankara on July 8, when he told Zelenskyy the US would allow Ukrainian production to begin. The about-face comes just two days after Trump and Zelenskyy met again, on July 28, and discussed reviving peace talks with Russia alongside the Patriot production plan; Zelenskyy had called that meeting 'good'. Defense analysts note that even a full go-ahead would likely take **years** to produce a single missile, since it requires transferring complex US technology, components, and training a workforce from scratch — so today's hesitation mainly matters as a political signal, not an immediate battlefield change.
key_points: Trump now says he **has not decided** whether to grant Ukraine a license to manufacture **Patriot interceptor missiles** domestically.
He called the Patriot an **'extraordinary weapon'** and said the US has **'to be a little bit careful'** about who it licenses the technology to.
This directly **contradicts his own announcement** from the NATO summit in Ankara on July 8, where he said the US would let Ukraine build the missiles.
The reversal comes just **two days after** a White House meeting with Zelenskyy where the two discussed 'Patriot interceptor production and several other ideas'.
Experts already warned any Ukrainian production **could take years** to materialize even if approved, since it needs US components, technology transfer and a trained workforce.

depth.background: The **Patriot air-defense system** is one of the few weapons capable of shooting down the ballistic missiles Russia has been firing at Ukrainian cities. Demand for its interceptor missiles has **outpaced global production**, partly because the US has also been supplying them to the Middle East. In July, at a **NATO summit in Ankara**, Trump surprised observers by promising Zelenskyy that Ukraine would get a license to build its own Patriot interceptors — a major ask Zelenskyy had been pushing for. The missiles are made by US defense contractors **Lockheed Martin and RTX Corporation**, who Trump admitted at the time had not even been informed of his announcement.

stories.title: India's pharma industry hits back at Trump's 100% drug tariff, says it will hurt American patients more than Indian exporters
stories.what_happened: Following the **100% tariff on patented drugs** taking effect in the US, **India's pharmaceutical industry pushed back strongly**, with leaders arguing the move could **hurt American patients more than Indian exporters**. Industry representatives pointed out that **India supplies nearly 47% of the US's generic drug needs**, meaning cutting off or taxing that supply would likely **raise the cost of treatment and medical procedures for American citizens**, not just squeeze Indian companies. India's pharmaceutical exports to the US are valued at roughly **$30 billion**, a market industry leaders say is significant but not irreplaceable — several noted India could **redirect more of its exports to Europe and other markets** and remain resilient. The reaction reflects broader unease in India's export sector about a series of Trump administration tariff moves affecting Indian goods over the past year.
key_points: Indian pharma industry leaders say Trump's tariff move **'may backfire'** and hurt US healthcare more than India's economy.
India supplies close to **47% of the US's generic drug needs**, making it the backbone of affordable medicine there.
India's pharmaceutical exports to the US are worth roughly **$30 billion**, putting that market squarely in the tariff's spotlight.
Industry voices argue the **cost of treatment and medical procedures in the US will rise**, hitting American citizens directly.
Some industry leaders say India can **redirect exports to Europe and other markets** and 'bounce back' even if the tariff bites.

depth.background: The tariff at the center of this reaction is the **100% 'Section 232' tariff** on patented pharmaceutical imports that took effect in the US today (see the linked global story) — though it mainly hits large branded drugmakers that lack pricing deals with Washington, not the **generic drugs** that make up the bulk of India's pharma exports. Still, India is the world's largest supplier of generic medicines, and its industry has been closely watching every US tariff signal since Trump's broader trade actions against Indian goods began. India's pharmaceutical sector is one of the country's largest export industries and a source of national pride as the 'pharmacy of the world.'

stories.title: Delhi Capitals gatecrash the Hardik Pandya trade race, offering Axar Patel and Prithvi Shaw for the MI captain
stories.what_happened: **Delhi Capitals have reportedly entered the race** to acquire **Hardik Pandya** from Mumbai Indians, emerging as the new front-runners according to reports, after the previously front-running **Chennai Super Kings deal reportedly stalled**. DC are said to be willing to part with **captain Axar Patel and opening batter Prithvi Shaw** as the core of a trade package for Pandya. This is a shift from the CSK-centered negotiations, where **Mumbai Indians had been demanding Shivam Dube and Ayush Mhatre** in exchange, while CSK instead proposed a package of **Dube, Dewald Brevis, and roughly ₹10 crore in cash**. As of now, **no deal has been officially confirmed** by any of the three franchises involved, and the saga remains a fast-moving, multi-team negotiation ahead of IPL 2027.
key_points: **Delhi Capitals** have reportedly emerged as new **front-runners** to acquire Mumbai Indians captain **Hardik Pandya**.
DC are said to be willing to give up **captain Axar Patel and opening batter Prithvi Shaw** as part of the trade package.
This comes after reports that Pandya's earlier proposed move to **Chennai Super Kings had stalled**.
Separately, **Mumbai Indians** have been demanding **Shivam Dube and Ayush Mhatre** from CSK, who instead offered Dube, Dewald Brevis, and cash.
**No trade has been officially confirmed** by any franchise — this remains an active, evolving negotiation.

depth.background: The **Indian Premier League (IPL)**'s trade window lets franchises exchange contracted players between seasons, subject to league approval — a relatively recent mechanism compared to the auction system that traditionally stocked squads. **Hardik Pandya**, Mumbai Indians' captain and a senior India all-rounder, has been at the center of trade speculation for weeks after a modest IPL 2026 season (206 runs at a strike rate of 138.26, with underwhelming bowling numbers). Chennai Super Kings had been the most talked-about suitor for months, floating various player-plus-cash packages, but Delhi Capitals' entry adds a new, potentially decisive competitor.

thread.previously: We reported that Chennai Super Kings had re-emerged as the front-runner to acquire Hardik Pandya from Mumbai Indians, offering a package built around Dewald Brevis plus cash, with KKR and RR also circling.
thread.changed: A new team has entered the race: Delhi Capitals are now reportedly the front-runners, offering to give up captain Axar Patel and opener Prithvi Shaw for Pandya, after the CSK talks reportedly stalled.
