stories.title: Bank of Japan holds its rate at 1%, but upgrades its growth forecast — keeping more hikes on the table
stories.what_happened: At its two-day meeting ending July 31, the Bank of Japan's policy board voted to **hold the short-term rate at 1%**, matching what most economists expected. In its quarterly Outlook Report, the bank **raised its fiscal 2026 GDP growth forecast to 0.8%** and nudged up its inflation outlook, signaling the economy is holding up better than feared. This was the first meeting since Japan and the US finalized a trade deal earlier in July, which removed a major cloud of tariff uncertainty hanging over Japanese exporters. Governor Kazuo Ueda's press conference comments were read as **cautious rather than hawkish** — he didn't commit to a specific date for the next hike. Most analysts now expect the BOJ to hold again in September and revisit a hike later in the year.
key_points: The BOJ kept its policy rate at **1%**, already the highest level since **1995**, at its July meeting.
It **upgraded its GDP growth forecast** for fiscal 2026 to **0.8%** in the quarterly Outlook Report.
This was the **first policy meeting since the new US-Japan trade deal**, which removed a big source of uncertainty.
The yen remains near a **40-year low**, which is part of why the bank keeps leaning toward tightening, not cutting.
Governor **Ueda struck a cautious tone**, tempering bets on exactly when the next hike lands.

depth.background: Japan spent decades with interest rates near zero to fight deflation. That changed through 2025 and 2026 as inflation finally took hold and the yen kept weakening, forcing the BOJ to raise rates repeatedly — to 0.75% in December 2025, then to **1%** in June 2026, the highest since 1995. A weak yen makes imports (energy, food) more expensive for Japanese households, which is why the central bank keeps nudging rates up even though higher rates also risk slowing growth and make Japan's enormous government debt costlier to service.

stories.title: India's Cabinet approves ₹84,084 crore 'Samudra Manthan' scheme to hunt for offshore oil and gas
stories.what_happened: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister **Narendra Modi**, approved the 'Samudra Manthan' (Ocean Churning) National Offshore Exploration Scheme on Friday, with a total outlay of **₹84,084 crore** to be spent through FY2030-31. The scheme has four components: **₹28,534 crore** for modern offshore seismic surveys to map likely reserves, **₹43,200 crore** to drill **60 deepwater exploration wells** — with the government covering up to 50% of each well's cost or ₹675 crore, whichever is lower — **₹10,000 crore** for shared offshore infrastructure hubs to help commercialize discoveries, and further funding to build a domestic offshore technology and manufacturing base under 'Make in India.' The government estimates the scheme could add more than **600 million tonnes of oil equivalent** to India's hydrocarbon reserves and cut annual crude oil imports by close to **₹1 lakh crore**.
key_points: The Cabinet approved **'Samudra Manthan'**, a **₹84,084 crore** national offshore exploration scheme running through **FY2030-31**.
It funds **60 deepwater exploration wells** (₹43,200 crore) and modern **offshore seismic surveys** (₹28,534 crore) to map the seabed for oil and gas.
The government will cover up to **50% of drilling costs per well** (capped at ₹675 crore) to de-risk exploration for companies.
The scheme targets adding over **600 million tonnes of oil equivalent** to India's proven reserves.
Officials say the extra output could cut India's crude **import bill by nearly ₹1 lakh crore a year**.

depth.background: India imports roughly **85% of the crude oil** it consumes, making it highly exposed to global oil-price swings and supply shocks — a vulnerability that's been on display this year as the US-Iran conflict pushed oil prices higher. Offshore exploration in Indian waters has lagged partly because deepwater drilling is expensive and risky, discouraging private companies from bidding aggressively. The government has previously tried to boost domestic output through auction reforms like the Open Acreage Licensing Policy, with mixed results. Samudra Manthan is the government's biggest single push yet to directly subsidize the riskiest, most capital-intensive part of that search: deepwater and ultra-deepwater drilling.

stories.title: Supreme Court blocks ruling that would have forced India's biggest stock exchange to answer RTI requests
stories.what_happened: On July 1, 2026, a Delhi High Court division bench of Justices C Hari Shankar and Om Prakash Shukla affirmed the CIC's long-standing 2007 finding that **NSE is a "public authority"** under the RTI Act, which would have opened the exchange's records to public information requests. NSE appealed to the **Supreme Court**, and on July 31 a bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta **stayed that High Court judgment**, issuing formal notice on NSE's appeal and ordering that the interim stay on the underlying 2007 CIC order continue **until further orders**. The effect is that, for now, NSE does not have to comply with the RTI obligations the High Court had just imposed, while the Supreme Court considers the full appeal.
key_points: The **Supreme Court** stayed a Delhi High Court judgment that had declared the **National Stock Exchange (NSE)** a "public authority" under the **RTI Act**.
A bench of Justices **Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta** issued notice on NSE's appeal and kept an interim stay in place "until further orders."
The dispute goes back to **2007**, when the Central Information Commission first ruled NSE must answer RTI requests because of its "deep and pervasive" government control.
The Delhi High Court had **upheld that 2007 ruling on July 1, 2026**, before the Supreme Court's stay effectively paused it again.
The case decides whether India's largest stock exchange, which handles trades for **millions of investors**, can be forced to publicly disclose its internal records.

depth.background: The **Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005** lets any Indian citizen demand information from a "public authority" — typically government bodies — to promote transparency and accountability. Whether a private-sounding entity like the **NSE**, India's largest stock exchange by trading volume, counts as a "public authority" has been fought over in Indian courts for nearly two decades, because exchanges perform an important public function (regulating and running the securities market) even though they aren't formally part of the government. The **Central Information Commission (CIC)**, the body that adjudicates RTI disputes, first ruled in 2007 that NSE qualifies because of the extensive regulatory control the government exercises over it.

stories.title: IMD issues a red alert for Gujarat as extremely heavy rain shuts schools; Arunachal Pradesh flags flash-flood risk
stories.what_happened: The IMD issued a **red alert for July 31** covering Ahmedabad, Vadodara, Anand, Bharuch, Narmada, Surat, Navsari, Valsad and several other Gujarat districts, forecasting **extremely heavy rainfall** with thunderstorms and gusty winds. In response, local administrations ordered educational institutions across the affected districts **closed for the day**. Separately, the IMD also warned of heavy to very heavy rain and a **flash-flood alert for nine districts of Arunachal Pradesh**, with isolated spots expected to see **12–20cm of rainfall within 24 hours** continuing into Saturday. State authorities in Gujarat have placed **13 districts on high alert** and are monitoring **39 flood-vulnerable villages** in Anand district alone, while emergency response teams have begun evacuations in the most exposed zones.
key_points: The **India Meteorological Department (IMD)** issued a **red alert** for **Ahmedabad, Vadodara, Surat** and other central and south Gujarat districts for July 31.
Gujarat district administrations ordered **schools and colleges shut** as a preventive measure against the extreme rainfall.
IMD separately warned of **flash floods in nine districts of Arunachal Pradesh**, forecasting **12–20cm of rain in 24 hours** in isolated spots.
This is a **different rain system** from the Odisha–Chhattisgarh–Madhya Pradesh depression covered a day earlier — Gujarat and the northeast are now the focus.
Emergency teams have been mobilized and evacuations have begun in flood-vulnerable areas.

depth.background: India's **monsoon season** (roughly June–September) brings the bulk of the country's annual rainfall, but the same system that provides essential water for agriculture also regularly produces destructive flooding. The IMD uses a **color-coded alert system** — red being the most severe, meaning 'take action' — to warn state governments and the public. Gujarat and India's northeastern states are both prone to monsoon extremes, but from different weather drivers: Gujarat typically sees intense bursts tied to depressions moving in from the Arabian Sea, while the northeast gets heavy orographic rain as monsoon winds hit the Himalayan foothills.

stories.title: 9 dead as a four-storey building — already flagged as dangerous — collapses in Bhiwandi near Mumbai
stories.what_happened: The four-storey Kohinoor Building in Bhiwandi's Balaji Nagar area, which housed 48 rooms across its floors, collapsed at around **11:30pm on Thursday, July 30**. Residents had heard loud cracking sounds roughly two hours earlier and started helping each other evacuate, but the building's 'B' wing came down while some occupants were still inside or on their way out. At least **9 people have been confirmed dead**, with rescue operations still underway as authorities fear more may be trapped under the rubble. The building had reportedly been declared dangerous by the local civic body, and repair work was in progress at the time it fell. NDRF and SDRF teams are using heavy equipment to clear debris, hampered by darkness and the scale of the wreckage.
key_points: The **Kohinoor Building** in Bhiwandi (Thane district) collapsed late Thursday night, killing at least **9 people**.
The building had earlier been **declared dangerous** by the local civic body, yet residents were still living there.
Repair work was reportedly underway when the structure gave way.
Residents heard **loud cracking sounds around 9pm** and began evacuating — but the 'B' wing collapsed around **11:30pm** before everyone got out.
**NDRF and SDRF teams** are digging through rubble in the dark; more people are feared trapped.

depth.background: Bhiwandi, a textile-manufacturing town in Maharashtra's Thane district near Mumbai, has one of India's highest concentrations of old, structurally weak buildings, many built without proper approvals decades ago. Monsoon season — when heavy rain weakens foundations — is when such 'dangerous' buildings most often give way, and this is one of several building-collapse tragedies the region has seen in recent years despite civic bodies formally flagging unsafe structures. The gap between a building being **officially declared dangerous** and it actually being vacated or repaired is a recurring failure in Indian urban safety enforcement.

stories.title: Rajya Sabha passes the anti-paper-leak bill amid an opposition walkout over the NEET leaks and Delhi crackdown
stories.what_happened: The **Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026** passed the **Rajya Sabha** (India's upper house of Parliament) on Thursday, July 30, a day after clearing the **Lok Sabha** (the lower house) on Wednesday. The bill strengthens India's 2024 anti-cheating law by adding **stricter penalties, mandatory time-bound investigations, and dedicated Special Fast Track Courts** to handle paper-leak and exam-fraud cases. During the debate, **Congress MP Mallikarjun Kharge** led criticism of the government over the recent **NEET paper leak** and its handling of the **July 20 crackdown on student protesters** in Delhi. Opposition MPs **walked out of the Rajya Sabha before the final vote**. Union Minister **Jitendra Singh** said the newly empowered Special Task Force will be required to complete its investigations within **2–3 months**. The bill now heads to the **President of India** for formal assent before becoming law.
key_points: The **Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026** cleared the **Rajya Sabha on Thursday**, a day after passing the Lok Sabha.
It adds **stricter penalties, time-bound investigations, and Special Fast Track Courts** to punish cheating and paper leaks in government exams.
**Opposition MPs, led by Mallikarjun Kharge, walked out** before the vote, criticizing the government's handling of the **NEET paper leak and a July 20 Delhi protest crackdown**.
A **Special Task Force** will now be required to complete paper-leak investigations within **2–3 months**, per the government.
The bill now goes to the **President for assent** before it becomes law.

depth.background: Paper leaks — cases where question papers for major government and entrance exams (like **NEET**, the medical-college entrance test) are stolen and sold or shared before the exam — have repeatedly disrupted Indian recruitment and admissions in recent years, forcing exam cancellations and derailing the futures of lakhs of students. India already passed a **Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act** in 2024 to criminalize this, but enforcement gaps remained, particularly around investigation timelines and specialized courts. This amendment tightens that framework. It comes against the backdrop of ongoing anger over the recent NEET leak and a controversial **July 20 police crackdown on student protesters in Delhi**, which the opposition has been demanding answers on.

stories.title: Coinbase posts a $359 million loss as a crypto-market slump bites harder than Wall Street expected
stories.what_happened: Coinbase reported a **net loss of $359 million** for the second quarter of 2026, badly missing analyst expectations of a roughly break-even quarter, as **revenue fell to $1.22 billion** against a forecast of **$1.3 billion**. Transaction revenue came in at **$599 million** and subscription/services revenue at **$555 million**, both below both analyst estimates and year-ago levels. Chief Financial Officer **Alesia Haas** said spot trading volumes across the crypto industry fell **more than 20%** during the quarter while overall crypto market capitalization shrank by double digits, driving a **14% sequential drop** in Coinbase's total revenue. The stock dropped as much as **14% in after-hours trading** on the news. Coinbase did highlight bright spots: it said it gained overall crypto market share, kept derivatives trading volumes flat even as the wider market fell, held expenses below the midpoint of its own guidance, and said its prediction-markets product now exceeds $100 million in annualized revenue.
key_points: **Coinbase** reported a **Q2 2026 net loss of $359 million** (about **$1.36 per share**), far worse than the roughly break-even result analysts had forecast.
**Revenue fell to $1.22 billion**, missing Wall Street's **$1.3 billion** estimate.
Industry-wide **spot crypto trading volumes slid more than 20%** during the quarter, and overall crypto market value shrank by double digits.
The stock fell as much as **~14% in after-hours trading** following the release.
Despite the miss, Coinbase said it **gained crypto market share** and that its newer **prediction-markets business topped $100 million** in annualized revenue.

depth.background: **Coinbase** is the largest US-based cryptocurrency exchange, and its earnings are widely watched as a barometer for how healthy the broader crypto trading industry is. The company makes much of its money from **transaction fees** — a cut of every trade — so when crypto prices and trading volumes fall, as they did sharply through much of 2026's summer downturn, Coinbase's revenue is directly exposed. The company has spent the last two years trying to diversify into subscriptions, custody, and newer products like prediction markets to reduce that dependence on trading volume swings.

stories.title: Nearly 50,000 migrants cross into Spain's Ceuta enclave in 24 hours; at least 18 die, Spain sends in the army
stories.what_happened: Beginning Thursday, July 30, thousands of people — the vast majority Moroccan nationals — rushed the Ceuta border, many wading and swimming around the breakwater fence where it meets the sea at Tarajal beach. Spain's Interior Ministry estimated **almost 50,000 crossings in 24 hours**, compared with only 1,500–2,000 over the previous ten days combined. At least **18 people died**, some by drowning, others in the crush of the crossing itself. Spain's government said Thursday evening it would send in the **Armed Forces** to help the Civil Guard restore order, and Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, alongside Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska, was set to visit Ceuta on Friday. Ceuta's local government has warned the city cannot absorb an influx of this scale.
key_points: Spain's Interior Ministry says **almost 50,000 migrants** crossed from Morocco into Ceuta in a single 24-hour window — the **biggest surge since 2021**.
At least **18 people have died**, mostly by drowning or in a crush at the Tarajal breakwater, where many swam around the border fence.
Ceuta's population is only about **83,000**, so the influx briefly grew the city by roughly **50%** overnight.
Spain is deploying its **Armed Forces** to back up the Civil Guard, with PM **Pedro Sánchez** visiting Friday.
Local officials link the surge to a **Spanish Supreme Court ruling** that barred summarily returning migrants who arrive by sea without due process.

depth.background: Ceuta is a small **Spanish city on the North African coast**, bordering Morocco — one of only two land borders between the EU and Africa (the other being Melilla). Because it's Spanish (and EU) territory, it has long been a magnet for migrants trying to reach Europe, and periodic mass border-rush attempts have happened before, including a large one in 2021. Morocco normally polices its side of the border under an informal arrangement with Spain, so a surge this size suggests either a deliberate loosening of controls or a sudden breakdown of coordination between the two governments.

stories.title: Sudan's RSF leader orders his fighters to 'seize Khartoum' as a UN probe finds his campaign in Darfur amounts to genocide
stories.what_happened: The RSF released a video on **July 30** of Hemedti telling his fighters to retake Khartoum, a city the army had largely recaptured earlier in the war. The declaration came as Sudan's army launched one of its most intense aerial campaigns of the war, striking RSF positions across **North and West Kordofan** with warplanes and drones on July 30, hitting several towns including Um Badr, Sodari and Al-Nuhud. The offensive followed a surprise army ground operation on July 25–26 that captured several towns and secured the export road linking North Kordofan to Khartoum — a supply line both sides need. Sudanese forces say they destroyed dozens of RSF vehicles in the fighting. The escalation follows a UN Fact-Finding Mission report, released around July 9, that found the RSF's campaign of mass killings and gang rapes in Darfur meets the legal definition of **genocide**.
key_points: RSF commander **Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo ('Hemedti')** released a video ordering his forces to retake the capital, **Khartoum**
It follows a **UN Fact-Finding Mission** conclusion that the RSF's violence in Darfur amounts to **genocide**
Fighting has spread to **North and West Kordofan**, with Sudan's army launching heavy airstrikes on RSF positions
The army says it seized a **key supply road** linking North Kordofan to Khartoum after a late-July ground offensive
Sudan's civil war, now in its **third year**, has driven one of the world's largest displacement crises

depth.background: Sudan has been torn apart since April 2023 by a war between the country's regular army (SAF) and the paramilitary **Rapid Support Forces (RSF)**, two factions that jointly seized power in a 2021 coup and then turned on each other over control of a transition to civilian rule. The RSF, led by Hemedti, swept into much of Khartoum and the western Darfur region early in the war, driving out millions of civilians and besieging army-held cities. The army has since clawed back ground, and fighting has increasingly shifted to the central **Kordofan** region, a strategic corridor connecting Darfur to the capital.

stories.title: Ajinkya Rahane, hero of India's historic 2020-21 Australia Test win, retires from all cricket
stories.what_happened: Rahane announced his retirement from international and all forms of cricket in a video shared on social media, saying the timing felt right to move on after a career that began in 2013. He finishes with 5,077 Test runs at an average of 38.46 and 12 centuries from 85 Tests, 2,962 ODI runs at 35.26 with three hundreds from 90 ODIs, and 375 T20I runs from 20 matches. He also featured in 212 IPL matches across six franchises. His career's defining moment remains captaining India to a 2-1 Test series win in Australia in 2020-21 in Kohli's absence — a result still regarded as one of the greatest overseas performances by an Indian side.
key_points: Ajinkya Rahane announced his retirement from **all forms of international cricket** in an emotional video posted on social media.
He finishes with **5,077 Test runs** at an average of **38.46**, including **12 centuries**, across **85 Tests**.
He captained India to a **historic series win in Australia in 2020-21** (the Border-Gavaskar Trophy) while deputizing for an absent Virat Kohli.
He also played **90 ODIs** and **20 T20Is** for India, plus **212 IPL matches** across six franchises.

depth.background: Rahane made his India Test debut in 2013 and became known as one of India's best overseas batters, with standout centuries in tough away conditions, including a famous hundred at **Lord's**. He is most remembered for captaining a weakened Indian side — missing Virat Kohli, who left the tour after the first Test — to a stunning **2-1 series win in Australia in 2020-21**, widely regarded as one of Indian cricket's greatest achievements. He last played a Test for India in 2023 against the West Indies and had since fallen out of the national picture, though he stayed active in domestic cricket and the IPL.

stories.title: Parliament finishes clearing the bill making it a crime to insult 'Vande Mataram', sending it to the President
stories.what_happened: On **July 30**, the Lok Sabha passed the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026 by voice vote after a brief but heated debate, then adjourned for the day. The bill makes it a **criminal offence** to insult 'Vande Mataram', extending the same legal protection already given to the national anthem and flag. This followed the **Rajya Sabha's** passage of the same bill the previous day, July 29. With both houses now having cleared the legislation, it moves to **President Droupadi Murmu** for her assent, the final step before it becomes law. Opposition MPs protested during the debate, though the bill passed without a formal division.
key_points: Lok Sabha passed the bill by **voice vote** on July 30, a day after the Rajya Sabha cleared it.
The bill amends the **Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act** to cover 'Vande Mataram' alongside the anthem and flag.
It now goes to **President Droupadi Murmu** for assent to become law.
Opposition MPs protested amid **uproar** during the brief Lok Sabha debate.
Violating the law could now mean **criminal penalties** for insulting the song.

depth.background: 'Vande Mataram' is India's national song (distinct from the national anthem, 'Jana Gana Mana'), rooted in the freedom movement and long treated as a symbol of patriotic reverence, though never previously protected by the same criminal penalties as the anthem or flag. The government introduced the **Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026** during the ongoing Monsoon Session to close that gap. The **Rajya Sabha** (the upper house, whose members are elected by state legislatures rather than directly by voters) passed it on July 29; passage in the **Lok Sabha** (the directly elected lower house) was needed to complete Parliament's process.

thread.previously: We reported that the Rajya Sabha passed the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill on July 29, making disrespect toward the national song a punishable offence, amid opposition anger over the timing.
thread.changed: The Lok Sabha passed the same bill today by voice vote, meaning it has now cleared both houses of Parliament and only needs the President's signature to become law.

stories.title: US Senate blocks a second attempt to force Trump to end military action against Iran
stories.what_happened: On **Thursday, July 30**, the Senate voted **49-50** against discharging Senator Kirsten Gillibrand's resolution, which would have required Trump to pull US forces back from the Iran conflict unless Congress explicitly authorized continued action. Three Republicans — **Rand Paul, Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski** — voted with most Democrats to support it, while Democrat **John Fetterman** voted against it, showing the vote didn't break cleanly along party lines. This marks the **second war-powers resolution on Iran to fail in the Senate within two weeks**. Even if it had passed the Senate, the resolution would still have needed to pass the House and survive a near-certain presidential veto to take effect.
key_points: The Senate voted **49-50** to reject a war powers resolution that would have forced **Trump to withdraw US forces** from action against Iran without Congress's authorization.
It's the **second such resolution to fail in two weeks** — the Senate also blocked a similar measure in mid-July.
Three Republicans — **Rand Paul, Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski** — crossed party lines to support it; one Democrat, **John Fetterman**, voted against it.
The resolution, from Democratic Senator **Kirsten Gillibrand**, needed to bypass the Senate Foreign Relations Committee — the vote was on whether to force that discharge.

depth.background: The **War Powers Resolution** is a 1973 law meant to stop presidents from waging prolonged military action without Congress's sign-off — but Congress rarely uses it successfully, since a president can veto it and overriding a veto needs a two-thirds majority. The US has been conducting strikes against Iran as part of an escalating conflict that has also drawn in Israel and, this week, seen **Iran strike targets in Kuwait and Jordan**. Repeated attempts to force a withdrawal via this law have failed in 2026, reflecting how divided Congress is over how far US involvement should go.

stories.title: RBI orders banks to publish fixed-deposit rates upfront and stop offering different rates at different branches
stories.what_happened: On **July 30, 2026**, the RBI issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Second Amendment Directions, 2026**, tightening how banks set and disclose fixed-deposit rates. Banks must now publish their deposit rate schedule on their website **before** offering those rates, and must apply the **same rate** to similar deposits accepted on the same day across all branches. For bulk deposits — large deposits often individually negotiated — banks must upload the applicable rate online by **10:00 am** every business day, with a maximum **10-minute grace period**. The rules apply to **six categories of deposit-taking institutions**, from big commercial banks to urban co-operative banks, and come into force from **October 1, 2026**.
key_points: The **RBI's new Amendment Directions** require banks to publish their **fixed-deposit interest rate schedule on their websites** before offering those rates to customers.
Banks can no longer offer **different FD rates at different branches** for the same deposit type booked on the same day — rates must be uniform.
For **bulk deposits**, banks must upload rates online by **10:00 am** each business day, with only a **10-minute grace period**.
The rules cover **six types of lenders** — commercial, small finance, regional rural, payments, local area and urban co-operative banks — and take effect **October 1, 2026**.

depth.background: Until now, Indian banks could offer **different fixed-deposit (FD) interest rates** for similar deposits depending on the branch, or informally negotiate special 'bulk deposit' rates with big depositors — making it hard for ordinary savers to know if they were getting a fair rate. The RBI first floated these changes as a **draft circular on June 5, 2026**, inviting public and industry feedback, and has now finalized them as binding rules after incorporating that feedback.

stories.title: Microsoft posts the biggest single-day market-value gain in stock market history — $450 billion in one day
stories.what_happened: On July 30, Microsoft reported fiscal fourth-quarter earnings showing Azure cloud revenue grew **43% year-over-year**, its fastest growth rate since early 2022 and ahead of what analysts expected. Management guided for **45% Azure growth** in the current quarter, above the roughly 41% Wall Street had penciled in. Shares closed up more than **15%** on the day, adding about **$450 billion** in market value — the biggest single-day dollar gain for any company in stock market history, surpassing Nvidia's $441 billion gain from April 2025. Microsoft's total market capitalization climbed to roughly **$3.35 trillion**. Nadella noted that Azure's annual revenue crossed $100 billion for the first time in fiscal 2026.
key_points: Microsoft shares jumped more than **15%** in a single session, adding roughly **$450 billion** in market value — the **largest one-day gain for any stock ever**.
It beat Nvidia's previous record of a **$441 billion** one-day gain from April 2025.
The surge followed earnings showing **Azure cloud revenue grew 43%**, its fastest pace since early 2022.
Microsoft's market capitalization now stands at about **$3.35 trillion**.
CEO **Satya Nadella** said Azure revenue topped **$100 billion** for a full fiscal year for the first time.

depth.background: Microsoft is one of the world's most valuable public companies, and in recent years that value has increasingly hinged on **Azure**, its cloud-computing business, and its massive bet on AI infrastructure. Investors across the market have been anxious about whether the hundreds of billions of dollars Big Tech companies are pouring into AI data centers and chips will actually pay off, or whether it's an **AI bubble** waiting to deflate. Every earnings report from a company like Microsoft is now read as evidence for one side or the other of that debate.

stories.title: Sensex and Nifty edge higher as auto earnings offset rising bond yields and pricier oil
stories.what_happened: India's benchmark **Sensex** index closed **0.4% higher at 77,928**, and the **Nifty 50** added **0.3% to 24,317** on July 30. Auto stocks led the gains: **Mahindra & Mahindra rose 2.2%** on strong June-quarter results, while **Maruti Suzuki and Tata Motors** each added **1.6%**. On the losing side, **Adani Ports fell 3.41%**, with Eternal (Zomato's parent) and UltraTech Cement also down. The gains came despite rising borrowing costs at the longer end of the bond market and higher energy prices, after the **US Federal Reserve** held interest rates but revealed hawkish dissent among its officials, and a contentious press conference by the Fed chair pushed up yields on inflation-protected US bonds.
key_points: Sensex rose **0.4% to 77,928**; Nifty added **0.3% to 24,317**.
**Mahindra & Mahindra jumped 2.2%** after strong June-quarter results; Maruti Suzuki and Tata Motors both gained **1.6%**.
**Adani Ports fell 3.41%**, the day's biggest loser, alongside Eternal and UltraTech Cement.
Indian bond yields rose after the **US Fed held rates** but flagged hawkish dissent.
A **contentious press conference** by the Fed's chair added to global bond-market volatility.

depth.background: Indian markets often take cues from both domestic company earnings and overnight moves in the US, since foreign investors move money between the two. This week's US Federal Reserve meeting — where it held interest rates steady despite some officials wanting a hike — has been rattling bond markets globally, including in India. At the same time, Indian companies are in the middle of reporting **June-quarter (Q1 FY27)** earnings, giving investors fresh, country-specific reasons to buy or sell individual stocks regardless of the global mood.

stories.title: India sweeps both team golds at the Commonwealth Table Tennis Championships in Delhi
stories.what_happened: India's men's table tennis team edged Malaysia **3-2** in a tense final to successfully defend the team gold it won in 2022, fielding Manav Thakkar, Manush Shah, G. Sathiyan, Harmeet Desai, and Payas Jain. The women's team was more dominant, sweeping Malaysia **3-0** with a squad of Sreeja Akula, Swastika Ghosh, Yashaswini Ghorpade, Syndrela Das, and Sutirtha Mukherjee. Both finals were played Thursday at the Thyagaraj Sports Complex in New Delhi, part of a championship running July 27 through August 2, 2026, that marks the tournament's return after a seven-year gap.
key_points: India's **men's and women's** teams both won gold at the Commonwealth Table Tennis Championships in New Delhi.
The men's team beat Malaysia **3-2** in a close final; the women's team won **3-0**.
It's a **title defense** for the men, who won gold at the last edition in 2022.
The tournament runs **July 27-August 2** at the Thyagaraj Sports Complex — separate from the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.
Key names: **Sreeja Akula, Sutirtha Mukherjee** (women); **Manav Thakkar, G. Sathiyan** (men).

depth.background: The Commonwealth Table Tennis Championships is a standalone event, distinct from the main Commonwealth Games currently underway in Glasgow — table tennis isn't part of that program this cycle, so this Delhi-hosted championship is the sport's own showcase for Commonwealth nations. It's returning for the first time since 2019 (the last edition was held in Cuttack, India). India has been a dominant force in Commonwealth table tennis, and hosting on home soil in Delhi added extra pressure and support for the squads.

stories.title: Delhi government agrees to drop legal action against NEET paper-leak protesters — with one carve-out
stories.what_happened: In a submission to the courts on July 30, the Delhi government stated it does not propose to take any further adverse legal action against individuals involved in the NEET paper-leak protests, and that the matter — including 13 cases registered by Delhi Police as of July 29 — 'shall be treated as closed without any future proceedings.' The one exception: this protection does not extend to anyone with prior criminal antecedents, in line with the Supreme Court's earlier order on the same protests. The climbdown follows weeks of pressure, including the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan and a rights-groups' outcry over the police response, and comes as Parliament's Monsoon Session continues to see opposition parties press the government over the same episode.
key_points: Delhi govt says it will take **no further legal action** against NEET paper-leak protesters and treat the matter as **closed**.
The one condition: protection **won't extend to protesters with a criminal record**, as required by the Supreme Court's order.
**13 cases** registered by Delhi Police over the Jantar Mantar protests will have their status reviewed as a result.
The protests followed a **May 2026** NEET-UG paper leak that forced **over 2 million students** to retake India's medical entrance exam.

depth.background: NEET-UG is India's single national entrance exam for medical college admission, taken by millions of students each year. In May 2026, allegations that its question paper had leaked forced the National Testing Agency to cancel results and make more than two million students sit the exam again — triggering intense stress that local media linked to several student suicides. Protests grew through the summer, culminating on July 20 when a march toward Parliament by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) was blocked by police, leading to what protesters called an unnecessarily forceful 'lathi-charge' and a temporary suspension of Delhi Metro and mobile internet in the area.

thread.previously: We reported the Supreme Court declined to ban pellet guns outright but ordered Delhi to ensure protesters injured by them get proper medical treatment, amid the fallout from the NEET paper-leak protests and a deadly police 'lathi-charge' (baton-charge) at Jantar Mantar.
thread.changed: The Delhi government has now told courts it will not pursue any further legal action against people involved in the protests, and will treat the matter as closed — except for anyone with a prior criminal record, per the Supreme Court's own order.
